gist: Joe Lonsdale interviews Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael on the Pentagon's six consolidated critical-technology priorities, its $200B Office of Strategic Capital loan program, Golden Dome missile defense, and AI-enabled targeting (Epic Fury), then shifts to a cybersecurity-focused segment (consistent with the FireEye/Mandiant background flagged in the intro as Kevin Mandia) on how AI is about to shift cyberwarfare from human-led to agent-led offense and defense.

themes.theme: AI-Enabled Warfare and the OODA Loop

insights.claim: The Epic Fury AI-enabled targeting program represents a leapfrog in applying AI to the military targeting-and-fires process, cutting through the fog of war to strike before an adversary can respond, but current capability shown publicly still has another 10x-100x of improvement ahead as AI models and infrastructure advance.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: Signals that current publicized military AI capability is an early, not mature, stage -- defense-tech investors should expect continued rapid capability jumps in AI-enabled targeting systems.
insights.quote: I I would say it it Epic Fury is a leapfrog in capability, but I think it also shows that there is another 10x 100x to go that's illuminated by what's already been done here.

insights.claim: Military AI applications are best understood as accelerating the classic OODA loop (Boyd's Observe-Orient-Decide-Act) rather than introducing something categorically new -- whichever side completes the loop fastest wins.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: A durable mental model for evaluating any new defense-AI announcement: ask whether it meaningfully compresses the observe-orient-decide-act cycle relative to adversaries.

insights.claim: Autonomous weapons have existed since the 1970s-80s (e.g., the Aegis missile-defense system, which fires automatically against an incoming missile because there's no time for human sign-off) -- today's AI-autonomy debate is more a difference of degree than of kind, and framing it as a total difference in kind produces distorted public conversations.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: Reframes the 'killer robot' policy debate around incremental risk calibration rather than a binary autonomy switch, relevant to how Congress and defense-tech companies should approach AI weapons regulation.

insights.claim: It is inevitable that AI agents run by 'the good guys' on offense will be used to train and harden AI-driven autonomous cyber defense -- the department is deliberately building offensive AI capability specifically to prepare defensive systems for an AI-agent-led attack environment.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: Signals a coming government-backed demand wave for offensive-capability cyber AI tooling used purely for defensive hardening -- relevant to cyber-defense contractors and startups.

insights.claim: Modern wars are empirically far less lethal than historical wars (roughly 70 million WWII deaths versus today's conflicts measured in hundreds), a trend partly attributable to precision- and AI-enabled targeting -- but this does not let humans off the hook, since the will to prevail in war will always ultimately depend on humans willing to fight.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the idea that robotics/AI eliminates the human and moral cost of warfare, a framing relevant to how defense policy debates AI deterrence claims.

insights.claim: The Department consolidated its list of congressionally mandated critical-technology areas from 14 down to six -- applied AI, intelligence analysis, AI-enabled war-fighting/command-and-control, contested logistics, biomanufacturing, and quantum/battlefield-information-dominance, plus scaled hypersonics and scaled directed energy called out separately -- to give a sprawling department actionable daily focus.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: Gives defense-tech investors a concrete, official roadmap of the exact technology categories the Pentagon will prioritize funding into over the coming years.

insights.claim: Biomanufacturing is being pursued for defense uses beyond medicine -- biological processes are being explored to separate rare-earth metals and produce energetics (TNT, gunpowder); portfolio company Cambium reportedly produces 'the best heat shielding in the world' using a bio-manufacturing technique.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, named company and use case (bio-manufactured heat shielding) that illustrates a defense-relevant biotech investment thesis outside pharma.

insights.claim: Quantum is included in the critical-technology list primarily for quantum sensing (battlefield detection and communication), not quantum computing, positioning it alongside radar, radio, and satellite links as part of a contested 'information dominance' battlefield domain.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: Clarifies that defense-quantum spending priorities are near-term sensing applications, not speculative quantum computing -- relevant for quantum-tech investors reading government priorities.

themes.theme: Office of Strategic Capital and the Defense Industrial Base

insights.claim: The Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital has $200 billion available in government loans priced near Treasury plus 100 basis points, split evenly between $100B for defense-industrial-base components (solid rocket motors, brushless motors, batteries) and $100B for critical minerals, with 3-4 critical-minerals deals announced in just the prior 45 days.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: A concrete, large-scale government financing program that defense-industrial and critical-minerals companies can tap -- material for investors tracking beneficiaries of federal industrial-policy capital.

insights.claim: The loan program is designed to send a demand signal that crowds in private capital, since companies receiving government loans undergo private due diligence and become more accountable once they have outside shareholders -- the loans can stand alone but are structured to attract additional equity investment.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: Explains the mechanism by which government lending is intended to catalyze, not crowd out, private investment in the defense-industrial base.

insights.claim: The US has roughly 250 medicines currently on shortage domestically because pharmaceutical supply chains are offshored -- cited as a direct analog to the same 'sleepwalked into dependency' pattern the Department is now trying to reverse for critical minerals and defense components.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: A tangible, non-defense example used to justify the urgency of reshoring critical supply chains -- relevant to reshoring/onshoring investment themes broadly.

insights.claim: The Department's new 'commercial first' posture reverses historical practice: companies like Palantir, Anduril, and SpaceX previously had to sue the government to win their first major contracts because legacy prime contractors were sophisticated at protecting their incumbent position; the explicit goal now is to make litigation unnecessary for the next wave of new entrants.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: Signals a friendlier procurement environment for new defense-tech entrants going forward, reducing the historical litigation-driven barrier to entry that Palantir, Anduril, and SpaceX had to overcome.

themes.theme: Golden Dome, Hypersonics, and Directed Energy

insights.claim: Golden Dome, the administration's homeland missile-defense initiative modeled on Israel's Iron Dome but scaled for a much larger territory, will be a layered system spanning space, ground, and 'under-layer' defenses against threats from North Korea, Iran, Russia, and China, including a newly issued RFI for space-based interceptors.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: A concrete near-term government procurement opportunity (space-based interceptors RFI) relevant to space and missile-defense contractors.

insights.claim: True hypersonic missiles (Mach 5+ and maneuverable) are far harder to intercept than legacy ICBMs or the missiles Iran fired at Israel, which were fast but not maneuverable and not sustained at hypersonic speed; the Department already knows how to build its own hypersonics but must now do so more cheaply and at scale to serve as a deterrent against China.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: Clarifies that the hypersonics priority is a cost/scale manufacturing problem, not a technology-readiness problem -- relevant to which contractors can execute on volume production.

insights.claim: Directed-energy weapons (high-power microwave systems like Epirus, and lasers) are being scaled specifically to counter the drone threat around major 2026-2028 US events (World Cup, America's 250th anniversary, Olympics) and at the border, urgency heightened because drone-attack costs have fallen sharply since mass production driven by the Ukraine-Russia war.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: Ties a specific named company (Epirus) and a hard timeline (major 2026-2028 events) to near-term counter-drone procurement demand.

insights.claim: Cyber conflict is shifting from human-led to AI-agent-led offense and defense -- AI agents will have 'total recall,' coordinate with each other at machine speed, and eventually enable autonomous, no-human-in-the-loop cyber defense, though true autonomous defense capable of matching agent-speed attacks is still years away and is being actively developed now.
insights.speaker: Kevin Mandia, cybersecurity executive (ex-FireEye/Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Signals a structural, multi-year shift in enterprise cybersecurity spend priorities toward autonomous AI-driven defense platforms.

insights.claim: AI dramatically favors the cyber offense in the near term because the fight is asymmetric -- one person on offense can create work for millions of people on defense -- meaning attackers gain leverage faster than defenders can respond until autonomous AI-driven defense matures.
insights.speaker: Kevin Mandia, cybersecurity executive
insights.so_what: A clear framework for why cybersecurity budgets should be expected to rise: offense's AI-driven cost advantage forces continuous defensive re-investment.
insights.quote: One person on offense can create work for millions of people.

insights.claim: AI-native engineering teams are delivering far more than 10x productivity gains versus legacy teams (contrasted with having run 4,500 engineers at FireEye) -- citing over 100 code commits in a single day and a new product demo every two to three days as concrete throughput evidence.
insights.speaker: Kevin Mandia, cybersecurity executive
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified data point on AI's effect on software engineering throughput that investors can use to sanity-check productivity claims from AI-native startups.

insights.claim: AI will automate voice-based social engineering -- as little as 6 seconds of someone's recorded voice can already be used to convincingly impersonate them to a help desk, meaning spear-phishing and vishing attacks will become increasingly indistinguishable from genuine communications.
insights.speaker: Kevin Mandia, cybersecurity executive
insights.so_what: A concrete near-term corporate-security threat (voice-clone social engineering against help desks) that enterprises should be actively defending against now.

insights.claim: The only credible answer to 'are we secure?' is empirical red-teaming (paying real offensive operators to try to break in over 5-6 days) rather than compliance dashboards or four-quadrant risk charts, which CEOs don't trust or fully understand; this is expected to become continuous ('red team everything all the time') as AI compresses attacker dwell time toward microseconds.
insights.speaker: Kevin Mandia, cybersecurity executive
insights.so_what: A practical prescription for how enterprise boards should evaluate cybersecurity readiness, useful for anyone assessing a company's security posture as a diligence factor.

insights.claim: Frontier AI models differ in how easily they can be prompted to generate exploit code -- Claude is described as the most resistant, xAI's Grok easier to get to comply, and Chinese models potentially easier still -- but model-makers may still need to loosen some safety gating because criminal actors will use ungated models regardless, so legitimate defenders need access to equally capable, ungated frontier models for security testing.
insights.speaker: Joe Lonsdale (host) and guest
insights.so_what: Raises a policy tension relevant to AI-safety-focused investors and labs: overly strict model gating on offensive security tasks could leave legitimate defenders under-resourced relative to criminal actors using looser models.

insights.claim: The 'Theodore Hall' Manhattan Project analogy (a Harvard-trained physicist who leaked atomic-bomb secrets to the USSR believing mutual possession would guarantee world peace) is used to argue that AI-in-warfare decisions should remain with elected/accountable officials rather than being decided unilaterally by brilliant technologists, since good intentions do not guarantee good outcomes.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: Frames the governance philosophy behind why the Pentagon insists policy-makers (not technologists or frontier labs) retain final say over AI-in-warfare rules, relevant to how defense-AI companies should expect to engage with government oversight.
insights.quote: Every death since 1949 from communism, which is the year the Soviets got the bomb, you could say that blood is at least partially on Theodore Hall's hands.

insights.claim: The Department's 'commercial first' AI posture is deliberate: rather than building its own frontier AI model in-house for roughly $100 billion, it leverages existing frontier labs' continuing innovation at much lower marginal cost, prioritizing access to industry's best AI talent over duplicating it internally.
insights.speaker: Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering
insights.so_what: Signals continued and expanding government procurement demand for frontier AI labs' models rather than a competing sovereign model effort -- relevant to how Anthropic, OpenAI, and others should value government contracts.
